newsitem.title: USA: Albright to walk out but U.S. consul to be at rite.
newsitem.headline: Albright to walk out but U.S. consul to be at rite.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright reaffirmed on Tuesday her intention to boycott the swearing in of Hong Kong's new legislature, but an official said the United States would still be represented.

On the day the Clinton administration won a major victory in Congress for its China policy, Albright began a trip to Vietnam, possibly to Cambodia and then on to Hong Kong for ceremonies surrounding the handover of the British colony to Chinese rule.

China's decision to replace the elected Hong Kong Legislative Council with an appointed legislature was "unjustified" and therefore "I will not participate in the swearing-in ceremony," she said in an appearance before a leading foreign affairs organization.

Although Albright did not mention it to 1,600 clapping members of the Commonwealth Club of California, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters that in her stead, the U.S. consul general in Hong Kong, Richard Boucher, would attend the swearing-in ceremony.
He described the decision as a matter of pragmatism.
"(Boucher) has to work, for better or worse, with the new legislature. For practical reasons, he will go," Burns said.
The disclosure drew immediate criticism from a spokesman for Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

"We would be appalled if Mr. Boucher attended the swearing in of the provisional legislature. His attendance would completely undermine Secretary Albright's boycott. The point of the boycott is to withhold American recognition of an illegitimate body," spokesman Marc Thiessen said in Washington.
"For Mr. Boucher to be there is basically giving a wink and a nod to Beijing that this is really OK," he added.
The State Department announced recently that Albright would not attend the swearing in of the new Hong Kong legislature because it was appointed rather than chosen in free elections.
But until Tuesday there had been no public mention of having Boucher or anyone else take her place.

The new, Beijing-backed legislature takes over when the elected Legislative Council ceases to function at midnight on June 30. Burns said Albright expected to walk out of the handover ceremonies before the new legislature was sworn in.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair also announced plans to boycott the swearing in but many other governments say they will be represented by top-level officials.

Albright spoke to the Commonwealth Club just as the House of Representatives, by a vote of 259 to 173, rejected a measure that would have overturned Clinton's decision to extend for one year most favored nation (MFN) trade status for China.

Critics argued the benefits should be denied because of fears China would erode Hong Kong's liberties and because of China's human rights record, trade imbalance with the United States, tensions with Taiwan and sales of arms to unstable regions.
Albright expressed sympathy for these concerns and promised that the United States would defend its interests in its relations with China, whose human rights record she called "dismal."

She renewed a U.S. warning that relations with China would be affected by how Beijing handled Hong Kong. Her attendance at the handover ceremonies is intended to underscore U.S. support for democracy and free markets in Hong Kong.

But praising the House for backing trade benefits for China, she said there was no substitute for engagement with a country that is one of the world's largest markets and, "next to us, will probably be the world's most powerful country."
She asserted her desire to follow through with a planned visit to Cambodia later this week but said the trip remained uncertain because of security concerns over recent violence.

She said it was necessary to prosecute Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot on genocide charges stemming from the mid-1970s, when more then 1 million Cambodians were killed, but said "it is unclear to all of us where he is" despite reports he is in custody.
